newsitem.title: UK: NMDA key to persistent pain, study finds.
newsitem.headline: NMDA key to persistent pain, study finds.

text.p: U.S. researchers said they had made a fundamental advance in understanding the physiology of persistent pain by showing a molecular connection between the site of an injury and the chemical pain process.

Writing in the science journal Nature, Allan Basbaum of the University of California San Francisco and colleagues said they had found that NMDA receptors, known to be involved in pain, helped prolong pain messages using the peptide substance P and glutamate.
Both substance P and glutamate are found widely in the dorsal horn neurons -- nerve cells in the spine associated with pain sensations. They are released by noxious peripheral stimuli or severe pain.

Basbaum's group injected NMDA into rats' spinal cords and found it mimicked changes seen in persistent injury, producing not only pain but substance P in the dorsal horn neurons and structural changes in their dendrites.

Injecting AP5, a selective NMDA antagonist, blocked pain behaviour. Injections of substance P receptor antagonists such as Merck's CP-99,994, or Rhone-Poulenc Rorer's RP-67,580 reduced pain behaviour significantly, they wrote.
"This result raised the possibility that the pain behaviour produced by NMDA is generated in part by release of substance P from primary afferent C (pain') fibres," they wrote.
"Consistent with this hypothesis, neonatal treatment with the neurotoxin capsaicin, which destroys NMDA receptor-laden fibres, also significantly reduced the pain behaviour produced by NMDA."
They used electron microscopes to analyse what was going on at the cellular level, they found it likely that substance P was being recycled.
"These results indicate that release of substance P contributes to the behavioural and morphological changes produced by NMDA," they wrote.
A positive feedback network could be in operaton, they proposed. -- Maggie Fox, London Newsroom 44-171-542-8958
